proofs.proof_tex:
Put \(m_i=\mathbb E_d[X_{ai}]=2d_i-1\) and \(v_i=1-m_i^2=4d_i(1-d_i)\). First suppose that \(d\in(0,1)^p\), so every \(v_i>0\). For \(T\in\mathcal I_k\), define
\[
 \psi_T(X_a)=\prod_{i\in T}\frac{X_{ai}-m_i}{\sqrt{v_i}}.
\]
By product randomization, factors belonging to different coordinates are independent. Each standardized factor has mean zero and second moment one. Hence, for \(T,U\in\mathcal I_k\),
\[
 \mathbb E_d[\psi_T\psi_U]=\mathbf 1\{T=U\}.
\]
Indeed, when \(T\ne U\), a coordinate in \(T\triangle U\) occurs to the first power and contributes a zero factor to the product expectation. Expanding each centered product gives
\[
 \psi_T
 =\sum_{S\subseteq T}
 \frac{\prod_{i\in T\setminus S}(-m_i)}{\prod_{i\in T}\sqrt{v_i}}\,\phi_S.
\]
All sets \(S\subseteq T\) remain in \(\mathcal I_k\), because that family is downward closed. Thus \(\psi=A\phi\), where
\[
 A_{T,S}=\mathbf 1\{S\subseteq T\}
 \frac{\prod_{i\in T\setminus S}(-m_i)}{\prod_{i\in T}\sqrt{v_i}}.
\]
In any ordering compatible with inclusion, \(A\) is triangular and its diagonal entry in row \(T\) is \(\prod_{i\in T}v_i^{-1/2}>0\). Consequently \(A\) is invertible. Orthonormality and the definition of \(\Sigma_k(d)\) yield
\[
 A\Sigma_k(d)A^{\mathsf T}=I_q,
 \qquad
 \Sigma_k(d)^{-1}=A^{\mathsf T}A.
\]
This proves positive definiteness and also gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \Phi_k(d)
 &=\operatorname{tr}(A^{\mathsf T}A)
 =\sum_{T\in\mathcal I_k}\sum_{S\subseteq T}A_{T,S}^2\\
 &=\sum_{T\in\mathcal I_k}
 \frac{\prod_{i\in T}(1+m_i^2)}{\prod_{i\in T}(1-m_i^2)}
 =\sum_{T\in\mathcal I_k}\prod_{i\in T}r(d_i).
\end{aligned}
\]
The penultimate equality follows by factoring the sum over \(S\subseteq T\), and the last follows from
\[
 \frac{1+m_i^2}{1-m_i^2}
 =\frac{d_i^2+(1-d_i)^2}{2d_i(1-d_i)}
 =\frac1{2d_i(1-d_i)}-1=r(d_i).
\]
Grouping subsets by cardinality is precisely the elementary-symmetric representation
\[
 \Phi_k(d)=\sum_{j=0}^k e_j(r(d_1),\ldots,r(d_p)).
\]
If \(d_i=0\), then \(X_{ai}=-1\) almost surely, so the singleton column \(\phi_{\{i\}}\) equals minus the intercept column. If \(d_i=1\), it equals the intercept column. Since \(k\ge1\), both columns are retained; hence \(\Sigma_k(d)\) is singular and the extended-real definition gives \(\Phi_k(d)=+\infty\).

For the announced classical attribution, the marginal information matrix for \((1,X_i)\) is
\[
 M_i=\begin{pmatrix}1&m_i\\m_i&1\end{pmatrix},
 \qquad
 \operatorname{tr}(M_i^{-1})-1
 =\frac{1+m_i^2}{1-m_i^2}=r(d_i).
\]
Substitution into the cited downward-closed product-design identity gives exactly the same displayed formula.

Finally, the requested smallest exact check succeeds. For \(p=3\), \(k=2\), at \(d=(1/3,1/3,1/3)\), all three factors equal \(5/4\), and therefore
\[
 \Phi_2(d)=1+3\frac54+3\left(\frac54\right)^2=\frac{151}{16}.
\]
At \(d=(1/4,1/3,5/12)\), the factors are \(5/3,5/4,37/35\), so
\[
 \Phi_2(d)=1+\frac{1669}{420}+\frac{217}{42}=\frac{4259}{420}.
\]
Thus the early-kill calculation agrees with the identity.

By the trace identity, it is enough first to work on the open cube. For \(0<v<1\), direct differentiation gives
\[
 r''(v)=\frac1{v^3}+\frac1{(1-v)^3}\ge16,
 \qquad r(v)\ge1.
\]
Writing \(m=2v-1\), a second direct calculation gives the log-curvature identity
\[
 (\log r)''(v)
 =16\frac{1+3m^4}{(1-m^4)^2}
 =16+16\frac{m^4(5-m^4)}{(1-m^4)^2}ge16.
\]
This also verifies the stipulated curvature stress test.

For every nonempty \(T\in\mathcal I_k\), set \(f_T(d)=\prod_{i\in T}r(d_i)\), let \(a_T\) have coordinate \((\log r)'(d_i)\) on \(T\) and zero elsewhere, and let \(D_T\) be diagonal with coordinate \((\log r)''(d_i)\) on \(T\) and zero elsewhere. Differentiation gives
\[
 \nabla^2 f_T(d)=f_T(d)\{D_T+a_Ta_T^{\mathsf T}\}
 \succeq16\operatorname{diag}(\mathbf 1_T),
\]
where positivity of \(a_Ta_T^{\mathsf T}\), the displayed log-curvature bound, and \(f_T\ge1\) justify the inequality. Every coordinate belongs to exactly
\[
 C_{p,k}=\sum_{h=0}^{k-1}\binom{p-1}{h}
\]
retained nonempty subsets. Summing the Hessians in the trace identity therefore yields
\[
 \nabla^2\Phi_k(d)\succeq16C_{p,k}I_p
 \quad\text{for every }d\in(0,1)^p. \tag{1}
\]

We next locate the minimizer rather than assuming it from symmetry. Put \(\bar d=p^{-1}\sum_i d_i\). For \(1\le j\le k\), the arithmetic--geometric mean inequality applied to the \(\binom pj\) subset products gives
\[
 \frac{e_j(r(d_1),\ldots,r(d_p))}{\binom pj}
 \ge \exp\!\left\{\frac jp\sum_{i=1}^p\log r(d_i)\right\}.
\]
Here each coordinate occurs in exactly \(\binom{p-1}{j-1}\) products, and \(\binom{p-1}{j-1}/\binom pj=j/p\), which proves the exponent on the right. The function \(\log r\) is strictly convex by the displayed curvature identity, so Jensen's inequality gives
\[
 \frac1p\sum_{i=1}^p\log r(d_i)\ge\log r(\bar d).
\]
Consequently
\[
 \Phi_k(d)\ge\sum_{j=0}^k\binom pj r(\bar d)^j. \tag{2}
\]
If \(L<p/2\), feasibility implies \(\bar d\le L/p<1/2\). Since
\[
 r'(v)=-\frac{1-2v}{2v^2(1-v)^2}<0\quad(0<v<1/2),
\]
equation (2) is at least \(\sum_{j=0}^k\binom pj r(L/p)^j\). Equality forces \(\bar d=L/p\) and, already from strict convexity in the \(j=1\) term, \(d_1=\cdots=d_p=\bar d\). If \(L\ge p/2\), then \(r(d_i)\ge1\) for every coordinate, with equality only at \(d_i=1/2\); hence the trace identity is at least \(\sum_{j=0}^k\binom pj\), uniquely at \(d=(1/2)\mathbf 1_p\). Boundary points have infinite criterion by the trace lemma. Thus in both cases the unique minimizer is \(d^\star=u\mathbf 1_p\), and substitution gives
\[
 \Phi^\star=\Phi_k(d^\star)=\sum_{j=0}^k\binom pj r(u)^j.
\]

It remains to prove the global certificate. Integrating (1) on the segment from the interior point \(d^\star\) to any interior feasible \(d\) gives
\[
 \Phi_k(d)\ge \Phi_k(d^\star)+
 \nabla\Phi_k(d^\star)^{\mathsf T}(d-d^\star)
 +8C_{p,k}\|d-d^\star\|_2^2. \tag{3}
\]
When \(u=1/2\), symmetry of \(r\) gives \(r'(u)=0\), hence the gradient term is zero. When \(u=L/p<1/2\), all components of the gradient at \(d^\star\) equal the same negative number, while feasibility gives \(\sum_i(d_i-u)\le0\); their product is nonnegative. Dropping that term proves
\[
 \Phi_k(d)-\Phi^\star\ge8C_{p,k}\|d-d^\star\|_2^2.
\]
At boundary points this holds in the extended-real sense.

At \(d=(1/2)\mathbf 1_p\), every \(f_T=1\), every \(a_T=0\), and every active diagonal entry of \(D_T\) equals \(16\); hence \(\nabla^2\Phi_k=16C_{p,k}I_p\). If \(L\ge p/2\), the path \(d(t)=d^\star+t(e_1-e_2)\) is feasible for all sufficiently small \(|t|\), using \(p\ge2\). Taylor's theorem then gives
\[
 \lim_{t\to0}\frac{\Phi_k(d(t))-\Phi^\star}{\|d(t)-d^\star\|_2^2}=8C_{p,k}.
\]
No larger global quadratic coefficient can therefore hold on the feasible class, which proves sharpness in the stated regime.

For an interior dosage, use the triangular matrix \(A\) and the standardized products \(\psi_T\) constructed in the proof of the trace identity. Since \(\Sigma_k(d)^{-1}=A^{\mathsf T}A\) and \(A\phi(x)=\psi(x)\),
\[
 \phi(x)^{\mathsf T}\Sigma_k(d)^{-1}\phi(x)
 =\sum_{T\in\mathcal I_k}\psi_T(x)^2.
\]
For a single coordinate,
\[
 \left(\frac{x_i-(2d_i-1)}{\sqrt{4d_i(1-d_i)}}\right)^2
 =\begin{cases}
 (1-d_i)/d_i,&x_i=1,\\
 d_i/(1-d_i),&x_i=-1.
 \end{cases}
\]
At \(d=d^\star\), one has \(0<u\le1/2\), so every nonnegative factor in every subset product is simultaneously maximized by taking \(x_i=1\) for all \(i\). The maximum is therefore
\[
 \mu^\star
 =\sum_{T\in\mathcal I_k}\prod_{i\in T}\frac{1-u}{u}
 =\sum_{j=0}^k\binom pj\left(\frac{1-u}{u}\right)^j.
\]
All support points have positive probability because \(0<u<1\), so this algebraic maximum is also the essential maximum needed below.

Fix \(T\subseteq[p]\) with \(|T|=k\). Because \(Z_{ai}=(1+X_{ai})/2\), the retained polynomial
\[
 g_T(X_a):=\prod_{i\in T}Z_{ai}
 =2^{-k}\prod_{i\in T}(1+X_{ai})
 =2^{-k}\sum_{S\subseteq T}\phi_S(X_a)
\]
is a nonzero linear combination of columns of \(F\); every \(S\subseteq T\) lies in \(\mathcal I_k\). If no sampled unit activates every coordinate of \(T\), then \(g_T(X_a)=0\) for every row \(a\). Hence the nonzero coefficient vector having entry \(2^{-k}\) on each \(S\subseteq T\) and zero elsewhere belongs to the null space of \(F\), so \(\operatorname{rank}(F)<q\).

Under \(d^\star\), product randomization gives
\[
 \mathbb P_{d^\star}\{Z_{ai}=1\text{ for all }i\in T\}=u^k
\]
for each unit. Independence across the \(n\) units then gives probability \((1-u^k)^n\) that no unit realizes this activation. That event is contained in \(\{\operatorname{rank}(F)<q\}\), proving
\[
 \mathbb P_{d^\star}\{\operatorname{rank}(F)<q\}\ge(1-u^k)^n.
\]

Write \(\Sigma=\Sigma_k(d^\star)\) and \(w_a=\Sigma^{-1/2}x_a\). The trace lemma makes \(\Sigma\) positive definite. Product randomization across units and the definition of \(\Sigma\) imply that the \(w_a\) are independent and
\[
 \mathbb E_{d^\star}[w_aw_a^{\mathsf T}]=I_q.
\]
The causal coefficient vector remains distinct from its observed-law identifying functional. In fact, linear response and conditional centering give
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \mathbb E_{d^\star}[x_aY_a]
 &=\mathbb E_{d^\star}[x_ax_a^{\mathsf T}]\beta
   +\mathbb E_{d^\star}[x_a\epsilon_a]\\
 &=\Sigma\beta+
   \mathbb E_{d^\star}\!\left[x_a\mathbb E(\epsilon_a\mid F)\right]
 =\Sigma\beta.
\end{aligned}
\]
Division by the invertible \(\Sigma\) therefore proves, rather than defines, \(\beta=\Sigma^{-1}\mathbb E_{d^\star}[x_aY_a]\).
Moreover, the exact-leverage proposition and the finiteness of the Boolean support imply
\[
 \lambda_{\max}(w_aw_a^{\mathsf T})=\|w_a\|_2^2
 =x_a^{\mathsf T}\Sigma^{-1}x_a\le\mu^\star
 \quad\text{almost surely}. \tag{4}
\]
Apply the cited matrix Chernoff result with \(K_a=w_aw_a^{\mathsf T}\), \(R=\mu^\star\), and
\[
 \mu_{\min}=\mu_{\max}
 =\lambda_{\min}(nI_q)=\lambda_{\max}(nI_q)=n.
\]
Put
\[
 h_+(t)=(1+t)\log(1+t)-t,
 \qquad
 h_-(t)=t+(1-t)\log(1-t).
\]
Both functions and their first derivatives vanish at zero, while, on \(0\le t\le1/2\),
\[
 h_+''(t)=\frac1{1+t}\ge\frac23,
 \qquad
 h_-''(t)=\frac1{1-t}\ge1.
\]
Twice integrating these inequalities gives \(h_+(t)\ge t^2/3\) and \(h_-(t)\ge t^2/2\ge t^2/3\). Since
\[
 \frac1n\sum_{a=1}^n w_aw_a^{\mathsf T}
 =\Sigma^{-1/2}(F^{\mathsf T}F/n)\Sigma^{-1/2},
\]
the union of the cited weak upper- and lower-tail events contains \(G_n(\varepsilon)^c\). Thus
\[
 b_{n,\varepsilon}
 \le2q\exp\!\left\{-\frac{n\varepsilon^2}{3\mu^\star}\right\}
 =\delta_{n,\varepsilon},
\]
and of course \(b_{n,\varepsilon}\le1\), proving the stated minimum bound.

On \(G_n(\varepsilon)\), the definition of that event gives
\[
 (1-\varepsilon)\Sigma\preceq F^{\mathsf T}F/n
 \preceq(1+\varepsilon)\Sigma. \tag{5}
\]
Because \(0<\varepsilon<1/2\), both bounds are positive definite, so \(F^{\mathsf T}F\) is invertible there. Inverting (5), with reversal of Loewner order, yields
\[
 \frac1{n(1+\varepsilon)}\Sigma^{-1}
 \preceq(F^{\mathsf T}F)^{-1}
 \preceq\frac1{n(1-\varepsilon)}\Sigma^{-1}. \tag{6}
\]
On this event, the linear-response assumption gives
\[
 \widehat\beta_\varepsilon-\beta
 =(F^{\mathsf T}F)^{-1}F^{\mathsf T}\epsilon.
\]
Conditional centering and conditional homoskedasticity consequently imply
\[
 \mathbb E[\widehat\beta_\varepsilon-\beta\mid F]=0,
 \qquad
 \operatorname{Cov}(\widehat\beta_\varepsilon\mid F)
 =\sigma^2(F^{\mathsf T}F)^{-1}.
\]
Multiplying (6) by \(\sigma^2>0\) proves the asserted conditional covariance sandwich.

The event \(G_n(\varepsilon)\) is measurable with respect to \(F\). On it, conditional mean zero makes the conditional squared-error risk the trace of the displayed covariance. On its complement the estimator is identically zero, so its squared error is exactly \(\|\beta\|_2^2\). The two disjoint cases therefore give the exact unconditional decomposition
\[
 R_n(\beta,\sigma,\varepsilon)
 =\sigma^2\mathbb E_{d^\star}\!\left[
 \mathbf 1_{G_n(\varepsilon)}
 \operatorname{tr}\{(F^{\mathsf T}F)^{-1}\}\right]
 +\|\beta\|_2^2b_{n,\varepsilon}. \tag{7}
\]
Taking traces in (6), using \(\operatorname{tr}(\Sigma^{-1})=\Phi^\star\), multiplying by the indicator, and averaging gives
\[
 \frac{\sigma^2\Phi^\star}{n}
 \frac{1-b_{n,\varepsilon}}{1+\varepsilon}
 \le R_n(\beta,\sigma,\varepsilon)
 \le\frac{\sigma^2\Phi^\star}{n(1-\varepsilon)}
 +\|\beta\|_2^2b_{n,\varepsilon}.
\]
The coefficient-ball assumption replaces the final norm by \(B^2\). Finally, for \(0<\varepsilon<1/2\),
\[
 \frac1{1-\varepsilon}\le1+2\varepsilon,
\]
and substituting the Chernoff envelope for \(b_{n,\varepsilon}\) proves the last advertised upper bound. No distributional property of the noise beyond the two stated conditional moments has been used.

Under the fixed-dimensional assumption, \(q\), \(\mu^\star\), and \(\Phi^\star\) are fixed positive constants. For all sufficiently large \(n\), the condition \(n>36\mu^\star\log n\) holds and
\[
 \varepsilon_n=3\sqrt{\frac{\mu^\star\log n}{n}}<\frac12,
 \qquad
 \varepsilon_n\longrightarrow0.
\]
The risk theorem gives
\[
 b_{n,\varepsilon_n}
 \le2q\exp\!\left\{-\frac{n\varepsilon_n^2}{3\mu^\star}\right\}
 =2qn^{-3}. \tag{8}
\]
For an admissible \((\beta,\sigma)\), set
\[
 \rho_n(\beta,\sigma)
 =\frac{R_n(\beta,\sigma,\varepsilon_n)}{\sigma^2\Phi^\star/n}.
\]
This is well defined because \(\sigma\ge\sigma_{\min}>0\) and \(\Phi^\star\ge1\). Dividing the two-sided risk bound by its oracle scale gives
\[
 \frac{1-b_{n,\varepsilon_n}}{1+\varepsilon_n}
 \le\rho_n(\beta,\sigma)
 \le\frac1{1-\varepsilon_n}
 +\frac{nB^2}{\sigma^2\Phi^\star}b_{n,\varepsilon_n}.
\]
The lower endpoint is below one by at most \(\varepsilon_n+b_{n,\varepsilon_n}\), and the first term of the upper endpoint exceeds one by at most \(2\varepsilon_n\). Uniformly over the stated coefficient ball, variance range, and all conditional-noise laws satisfying the two moment assumptions, (8) therefore yields
\[
 \left|\rho_n(\beta,\sigma)-1\right|
 \le2\varepsilon_n+2qn^{-3}
 +\frac{2B^2q}{\sigma_{\min}^2\Phi^\star}n^{-2}.
\]
The right-hand side is deterministic and tends to zero. Taking the displayed supremum proves the asserted uniform oracle attainment. Because the argument treats \(\mu^\star\) as fixed, it makes no growing-dimension or vanishing-supply uniformity claim.

When \(k=1\), the retained family consists only of the empty set and the \(p\) singletons. The trace identity immediately becomes
\[
 \Phi_1(d)=1+\sum_{i=1}^p r(d_i).
\]
The uniform-optimum theorem gives the unique optimizer \(d_i=u=\min\{L/p,1/2\}\), which is the uniform limited-supply dosage in the additive product-Bernoulli design. If \(L\ge p/2\), then \(u=1/2\) and \(r(1/2)=1\), so
\[
 \Phi^\star=1+p.
\]

added_lemmas.statement:
Let \(K_1,\ldots,K_n\) be independent positive-semidefinite random matrices of dimension \(q\), and suppose for a constant \(R>0\) that \(\lambda_{\max}(K_a)\le R\) almost surely. Define
\[
 \mu_{\min}=\lambda_{\min}\!\left(\sum_{a=1}^n\mathbb E K_a\right),
 \qquad
 \mu_{\max}=\lambda_{\max}\!\left(\sum_{a=1}^n\mathbb E K_a\right).
\]
For \(0<\varepsilon<1\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \mathbb P\!\left\{\lambda_{\min}\!\left(\sum_{a=1}^nK_a\right)\le(1-\varepsilon)\mu_{\min}\right\}
 &\le q\left[\frac{e^{-\varepsilon}}{(1-\varepsilon)^{1-\varepsilon}}\right]^{\mu_{\min}/R},\\
 \mathbb P\!\left\{\lambda_{\max}\!\left(\sum_{a=1}^nK_a\right)\ge(1+\varepsilon)\mu_{\max}\right\}
 &\le q\left[\frac{e^{\varepsilon}}{(1+\varepsilon)^{1+\varepsilon}}\right]^{\mu_{\max}/R}.
\end{aligned}
\]

source.locator: Corollary 5.2, Matrix Chernoff II, equations (5.1) and (5.2)
source.verbatim_statement: For independent positive-semidefinite self-adjoint matrices with uniform eigenvalue bound \(R\), Corollary 5.2 gives \(\mathbb P\{\lambda_{\min}(\sum_kX_k)\le(1-\delta)\mu_{\min}\}\le d[e^{-\delta}/(1-\delta)^{1-\delta}]^{\mu_{\min}/R}\) and \(\mathbb P\{\lambda_{\max}(\sum_kX_k)\ge(1+\delta)\mu_{\max}\}\le d[e^{\delta}/(1+\delta)^{1+\delta}]^{\mu_{\max}/R}\).

proposed.statement:
For every \(d\in\mathcal D_L\cap(0,1)^p\), the population Gram matrix is positive definite and
\[
 \Phi_k(d)=\sum_{T\in\mathcal I_k}\prod_{i\in T}r(d_i)
 =\sum_{j=0}^{k}e_j(r(d_1),\ldots,r(d_p)).
\]
If any coordinate of \(d\) equals zero or one, then \(\Sigma_k(d)\) is singular and \(\Phi_k(d)=+\infty\). The interior identity is obtained by the triangular change from the fixed monomials to product-orthonormal features and is the Bernoulli specialization of the downward-closed product-design identity of Schwabe and Wong.
proposed.justification: This representation removes the higher-order characteristic-polynomial obstruction and exposes separable curvature.
proposed.gap: SchwabeWong1999 contains the general identity, while ShyamalZhangUhler2025 does not specialize it to solve the shared-supply all-order problem.
proposed.consumer: The identity turns the interaction-design problem into an explicit scalar symmetric-polynomial optimization usable by the dosage theorem.

proposed_core_edits.reason: Declare the cited Schwabe--Wong identity that supports the target's explicit classical-attribution clause; the mathematical identity itself is also derived directly.

proposed.statement:
Under \(d^\star\), let \(b_{n,\varepsilon}=\mathbb P_{d^\star}(G_n(\varepsilon)^c)\). On \(G_n(\varepsilon)\), \(\operatorname{Cov}(\widehat\beta_{\varepsilon}\mid F)=\sigma^2(F^{\mathsf T}F)^{-1}\), and
\[
 \frac{\sigma^2}{n(1+\varepsilon)}\Sigma_k(d^\star)^{-1}
 \preceq\operatorname{Cov}(\widehat\beta_{\varepsilon}\mid F)
 \preceq\frac{\sigma^2}{n(1-\varepsilon)}\Sigma_k(d^\star)^{-1}.
\]
Unconditionally,
\[
 R_n(\beta,\sigma,\varepsilon)
 =\sigma^2\mathbb E_{d^\star}\left[\mathbf 1_{G_n(\varepsilon)}
 \operatorname{tr}((F^{\mathsf T}F)^{-1})\right]
 +\|\beta\|_2^2b_{n,\varepsilon}.
\]
Furthermore, \(b_{n,\varepsilon}\le\min\{1,\delta_{n,\varepsilon}\}\), where \(\delta_{n,\varepsilon}=2q\exp\{-n\varepsilon^2/(3\mu^\star)\}\), and
\[
 \frac{\sigma^2\Phi^\star}{n}\frac{1-b_{n,\varepsilon}}{1+\varepsilon}
 \le R_n(\beta,\sigma,\varepsilon)
 \le\frac{\sigma^2\Phi^\star}{n(1-\varepsilon)}+B^2b_{n,\varepsilon}.
\]
The upper bound also implies
\[
 R_n(\beta,\sigma,\varepsilon)
 \le\frac{\sigma^2\Phi^\star}{n}(1+2\varepsilon)
 +2B^2q\exp\{-n\varepsilon^2/(3\mu^\star)\}.
\]
proposed.justification: The theorem verifies the exact Chernoff constant and keeps the fallback bias in the unconditional risk.
proposed.gap: Tropp2012 supplies the tail tool and HsuKakadeZhang2014 supplies general decompositions, but neither gives this product-Fourier leverage calibration or fallback branch.
proposed.consumer: The bound converts the exact population design into an auditable finite-sample precision guarantee.

proposed_core_edits.reason: Declare the precise published matrix Chernoff result and the primitive randomization and population-information nodes used to verify all of its hypotheses.

open_obligations.what_is_open: An explicit finite-\(n\) comparison over \(d\in\mathcal D_L\) requires a dosage-indexed spectral event, estimator, bad-event probability, and unconditional risk, followed by solution of the resulting nonconvex finite-support optimization.
open_obligations.obstruction: The frozen objects \(G_n(\varepsilon)\), \(\widehat\beta_\varepsilon\), and \(R_n(\beta,\sigma,\varepsilon)\) are defined only using \(\Sigma_k(d^\star)\) and expectation under \(P_{d^\star}\). Thus the frozen core contains no well-typed objective map whose argument is a competing dosage \(d\), so no minimizer or frontier over \(\mathcal D_L\) can be proved without first adding that construction and specifying its threshold convention.
open_obligations.attempted: I substituted the exact conditional-risk decomposition, maximized its two nonnegative terms over the coefficient ball and variance interval, and reduced the assignment expectation to a finite Boolean-support sum. This closes the coefficient/noise saddle at \(d^\star\), but permutation symmetry does not compare different product dosages, and extending the estimator by silently replacing \(d^\star\) with \(d\) would change the frozen construction and the question's formal scope.
open_obligations.partial_result:
At the single dosage \(d^\star\) for which the frozen estimator and risk are defined, the proved decomposition gives the computable worst-case value
\[
 \sup_{\substack{\|\beta\|_2\le B,\ 
 \sigma\in[\sigma_{\min},\sigma_{\max}]\\
 \text{admissible conditional-noise laws}}}
 R_n(\beta,\sigma,\varepsilon)
 =\sigma_{\max}^2\mathbb E_{d^\star}\!\left[
 \mathbf 1_{G_n(\varepsilon)}\operatorname{tr}\{(F^{\mathsf T}F)^{-1}\}\right]
 +B^2b_{n,\varepsilon}.
\]
The equality follows because the two terms depend on \(\sigma^2\) and \(\|\beta\|_2^2\), respectively, with nonnegative coefficients, and admissible centered homoskedastic noise laws exist at every allowed variance. This settles the worst-case coefficient/noise optimization at \(d^\star\), but it does not define or compare the corresponding quantity at \(d\ne d^\star\).
